name: Design Metaphors
description:
Design metaphors use the characteristics of one domain to help imagine or explain another. A designer might ask how a service could behave like a library, ecosystem, conversation or marketplace and use relationships from that source domain to generate new possibilities.

Metaphors can support ideation and communication by making unfamiliar concepts easier to think about through familiar structures.
whenToUse: Use design metaphors when a team is struggling to move beyond existing conventions, when an abstract system needs to become easier to understand, or when alternative interaction models are being explored.
steps: Define the design problem or experience.
Identify its important qualities or relationships.
Select a metaphor and examine its components, behaviours and relationships.
Map potentially useful relationships onto the design problem.
Evaluate which resulting ideas are useful without forcing the final design to follow the metaphor literally.
lookOutFor: Metaphors highlight some relationships while hiding others.
A familiar metaphor may carry assumptions that do not fit the design situation.
Do not let the metaphor become a constraint once it stops being productive.

resources.citation: Lakoff, G. & Johnson, M. (1980). *Metaphors We Live By*. University of Chicago Press.
Erickson, T. D. (1990). “Working with Interface Metaphors.” In Laurel, B. (ed.), *The Art of Human-Computer Interface Design*. Addison-Wesley.
